posts.title: SpaceX’s million-satellite plan faces questions over pollution, safety and feasibility
posts.description: SpaceX Falcon Heavy Demo Mission (Photo by SpaceX on Unsplash) This week, on the eve the Thanksgiving holiday, the United States Federal Communications Commission approved SpaceX’s plan to launch one million “ Starmind ” artificial intelligence (AI) data centre satellites. This decision reflects the convergence of a satellite boom, an AI bubble and the Trump administration’s disregard for environmental regulation. If Starmind proceeds in full, the number of operational satellites will be multiplied by a factor of 50. Space and our night skies will become vastly busier places. SpaceX’s pitch is to take the impact of data centres away from Earth, using a million solar-powered satellites to do AI data crunching in space and beam the results to Earth. But what is the impact of one million satellites, both in space and on Earth? Why has the Federal Communications Commission made this decision? And will a million satellites actually end up in orbit? posts.title: Four percent of Nepal’s listed shares remain beyond the reach of Demat
posts.description: Kathmandu, November 27 Nearly 4 percent of the shares listed on Nepal’s stock market have yet to be dematerialised, leaving 846.8 million shares outside the electronic system even more than a decade after the introduction of mandatory Demat accounts. According to CDS and Clearing (CDSC), a total of 20.87 billion shares are currently listed on the stock market. Of these, 20.03 billion have been dematerialised, while 846.8 million remain unconverted into electronic form. This means the ownership records of around 4 percent of listed shares remain outside the Demat system. These shares cannot be traded on the secondary market, and their holders may also be unable to receive dividends until the shares are dematerialised. More strikingly, the number of shares yet to be dematerialised has continued to rise. Two years ago, around 750 million shares had not been converted into electronic form. posts.title: Government prepares special task force to curb foreign employment fraud
posts.description: Kathmandu, November 28 The government is preparing to form a special task force to tackle fraud and labour exploitation in foreign employment, including cases involving recruitment scams, workers being assigned jobs different from those promised, withheld wages and benefits, and human trafficking disguised as travel on visit visas. A high-level meeting chaired by Home Minister Sudan Gurung on November 20 decided to establish a task force involving relevant agencies to curb fraud linked to foreign employment and consultancy services. The Ministry of Youth, Labour and Employment is leading the process of forming the task force, which will include representatives from relevant government agencies. The meeting also decided to establish separate targeted teams within the Ministry of Education and Sports, Nepal Police, the Department of Foreign Employment and the Department of Immigration.
